prompt: Engineers changed their testing routine to fit a new crash-simulation tool; months later, the vendor changed the tool to fit that routine; then the routine shifted again.
tells: the vendor changed the tool to fit that routine; then the routine shifted again
why: Distinct human and material changes stack in sequence.
trap: The changes are separate and layered, not inseparable.

prompt: A study describes human routines and software features as separate agencies that overlap in layers over time, each new layer resting on the last.
why: That's Leonardi's image of interlocking tiles.

prompt: A sales team began meeting weekly to review the CRM's pipeline. Their meeting led IT to add a forecast view, which in turn changed who attended the meeting.
tells: which in turn changed who attended the meeting
why: Human and material changes build on each other over time.
trap: Affordance is one moment of possibility; this is a sequence.

prompt: Nurses created a charting routine; the hospital then built it into the EHR as a template; the template let a new handoff routine form on top of it.
tells: the template let a new handoff routine form on top of it
why: Layers of human and material agency stack.
trap: The template isn't a designer's script imposed from outside; it came from the routine.

prompt: A ward first added a daily huddle; IT then built a huddle dashboard; staff then reorganized the huddle to start from the dashboard's red items.
tells: staff then reorganized the huddle to start from the dashboard's red items
why: Routine, then tech, then routine: distinct layers over time.
trap: The sequence of separate changes is the tell.

prompt: A team started pairing on code reviews; the review tool then gained a live co-editing mode; that mode later led the team to drop its review meetings.
tells: that mode later led the team to drop its review meetings
why: Human and material changes stack in turns.
trap: No designer script or alliance-building; it's layered change.
